sections.h: Amos the book and the man
sections.b: Amos was a herdsman and tender of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah who spoke at Bethel in the reign of Jeroboam II, two years before an earthquake (Amos 1:1; 7:14). The book has nine chapters: oracles against seven nations (Judah among them) and then Israel, three sermons, five visions, the story of the priest Amaziah and a closing promise. See the book's opening pages for the outline and the debates over how it was put together.

Amos names the acts that make a society unjust: selling a person over a small debt, trampling the poor, taking bribes at the gate, and cheating with false measures (Amos 2:6-7; 5:12; 8:5-6). His best-known line asks that "justice roll like water" (Amos 5:24). The Hebrew word is mishpat, the right decision of a court and the order of a community, paired with tsedaqah, righteousness. Amos does not set up a new law; he points to the law Israel had (Exodus 22:26; Deuteronomy 24:12-13).

The poor appear as the victims of debt slavery, bribed courts, unfair rents of grain and rigged scales (Amos 2:6-7; 4:1; 5:11-12; 8:4-6). Amos uses four words for them: tsaddiq "the righteous" (in the right), evyon "the needy", dal "the poor" and anaw "the humble". He does not praise poverty as such; he condemns those who cause it.

Amos shows the wealth of Samaria: winter and summer houses, houses of ivory, beds of ivory, lamb and fattened calf, wine in bowls and the best oils (Amos 3:15; 6:4-6). The charge is not that the pleasures are evil but that they rest on the oppression of the poor and that the ruin of Joseph does not make them sick (Amos 6:6). Excavations at Samaria found carved ivory plaques of the period.

Amos 5:18-20 is the oldest passage in a prophetic book to use the phrase. His hearers longed for the day of the LORD; Amos says it is darkness and not light, like escaping a lion and meeting a bear. Compare 8:9-10, where the sun sets at midday. For Amos the day is a coming defeat of Israel, not the end of the world; Joel, Zephaniah and the New Testament give the phrase a wider sense.

Amos uses the idea in several ways: the few who will be left after the defeat (Amos 3:12; 5:3), perhaps the LORD will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph (Amos 5:15), and the promise that the LORD will not wipe out the house of Jacob completely (Amos 9:8). Scholars debate whether the hope is Amos's own or an editor's.

Bethel was the chief shrine of the northern kingdom and the place where Amos spoke. Amos mocks the pilgrimage ("Go to Bethel, and rebel", 4:4), forbids seeking it (5:5), says its altar will be cut down (3:14) and is told by its priest to leave because it is "the king's sanctuary" (7:13). Compare Hosea's pun on Beth-aven.

Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, is the setting of the sermons on wealth: the citadels of 3:9-11, the cows of Bashan on its mountain (4:1), the ivory houses (3:15) and the leaders who are secure on its mountain (6:1). The excavators found ivory plaques there.

Jeroboam son of Joash (about 793-753 BC) ruled Israel at its largest since Solomon (2 Kings 14:23-29). Amos is dated by him (1:1), the prophecy against his house is in 7:9, and Amaziah says Amos predicted his death by the sword (7:11), which 2 Kings 14:29 does not report. His victories at Lo-debar and Karnaim (6:13) are mocked.

Amos dates his words to the days of Uzziah of Judah as well as Jeroboam (Amos 1:1). Uzziah reigned 52 years (2 Chronicles 26) and the earthquake of his time is recalled in Zechariah 14:5. His breach of Gath's wall may explain why Gath is missing in Amos 1:6-8.

Amos charges Edom with chasing his brother with the sword and keeping his anger forever (Amos 1:11-12). The Hebrew of 9:12 has Israel possess "the remnant of Edom", where the Greek (and Acts 15:17) has "the rest of humankind". Obadiah develops the charge.

The first oracle is against Damascus for threshing Gilead with iron sledges, a reference to Hazael's wars (2 Kings 10:32-33; 13:3-7). The Arameans are to go into exile to Kir (Amos 1:5), and in 9:7 the LORD says he brought them from Kir.
Tyre is charged with delivering whole communities of exiles to Edom and forgetting "the brothers' covenant", probably the treaty of Hiram and Solomon (Amos 1:9-10; 1 Kings 5:12).

Ammon is charged with ripping open the pregnant women of Gilead to enlarge its land (Amos 1:13-15). The punishment is fire on the walls of Rabbah and exile of "their king" (or Milcom; see the variant).
Moab is charged with burning the bones of the king of Edom into lime, a crime against the dead (Amos 2:1-3). Fire falls on Kerioth.

Judah is the seventh nation in the series and gets the shortest charge: it has rejected the LORD's teaching and followed lies (Amos 2:4-5). Many scholars think the oracle is an editor's addition; others defend it for Amos. Amos himself is from Judah.

Gaza is charged with selling whole communities of exiles to Edom (Amos 1:6-8). Four of the five Philistine cities are named; Gath is missing. In 9:7 the LORD says he brought the Philistines from Caphtor, as he brought Israel from Egypt.

The five disasters of Amos 4:6-11 are the kinds of trouble the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 name, though not in this order: hunger, drought, blight, plague and war, and overthrow. The LORD calls Israel's refusal to turn back the reason for the next step.

Amos 3:2 says that out of all the clans of the earth the LORD has known Israel only, and so will call it to account for its guilt: election brings accountability. Amos 9:7 asks whether Israel is not like the Cushites to the LORD, and says that he also led the Philistines and Arameans. The two verses are read together or in tension.

sections.h: The LORD changed his mind in Amos
sections.b: In the first two visions the LORD "changed his mind about this" after Amos's prayer (Amos 7:3, 6). In the third and fourth he will not "overlook them any more" (7:8; 8:2). The Plain follows the wording of Exodus 32:14 and Jeremiah 18:8.
Amos twice accuses the leaders of turning justice into wormwood, a bitter herb (Amos 5:7), and into poison (rosh) with the fruit of righteousness into wormwood (6:12).

sections.h: The Sabbath and the New Moon in Amos
sections.b: The grain merchants are impatient for the New Moon and the Sabbath to pass so they can sell again (Amos 8:5). It shows that rest from trade on these days was kept, and that some who kept it hated it.

The LORD says "I hate your festivals" and that he will not enjoy the smell of your sacred gatherings (Amos 5:21-22) and will turn the festivals into mourning (8:10). The fault is not the festival but the place of injustice.
The high places of Isaac will be left empty and Israel's holy places laid waste (Amos 7:9). Amos opposes the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba (4:4; 5:5; 8:14).
Amos mocks the practice of bringing tithes "every three days" (Amos 4:4); the law asks for tithes by the year, and every third year for the poor (Deuteronomy 14:22-29).

sections.h: "For three ... and for four" in Amos
sections.b: Amos 1:3-2:6 use the pattern "for three rebellions of X, and for four" eight times. The model is the numerical proverb (Proverbs 30:15-33): the number is a way to say "enough, and more". Amos does not list the transgressions; he names one.

Amos 1:3-2:16 names seven nations, Judah among them, and then Israel, and uses the same pattern for the first seven: the messenger formula, the number formula, a crime, and fire (Israel's oracle has no fire). The crimes of the foreign nations are cruelties in war and trade; Judah's is rejecting the LORD's teaching; Israel's is a list of acts against the poor. Many see the series as a net drawn tight around Israel.

Amos says he is "no prophet" by trade and no prophet's son, but the LORD took him from the flock and told him to prophesy (Amos 7:14-15). He compares the LORD's call to a lion's roar: who can keep from prophesying? (3:8). He claims the prophet is told the LORD's counsel (3:7).

sections.h: The booth of David in Amos
sections.b: Amos 9:11 promises that on that day the LORD will raise up the fallen booth of David. The ancient readings differ: the Targum reads the booth as the kingdom of David's house; the Talmud names the Messiah Bar Nafle, "son of the fallen"; the Damascus Document and 4QFlorilegium each interpret it. Acts 15:16 quotes it.

James quotes Amos 9:11-12 (in the Greek form) to show that the Gentiles who turn to God do not have to become Jews (Acts 15:15-18). The Hebrew has Israel possess "the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by my name". Catholic, Reformed, dispensational and evangelical readers differ on what the "booth of David" is and when it is raised.

Acts quotes Amos twice, in Stephen's speech (Acts 7:42-43 on Amos 5:25-27, with Babylon for Damascus) and in James's speech at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:15-18 on Amos 9:11-12). Both follow the Greek form.

Amos 9:7 asks "Are you Israelites not like the Cushites to me?" Cush is a far land to the south of Egypt. The verse puts Israel beside a people at the edge of the known world, and sets the exodus beside the LORD's leading of the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir.
Carmel is a green mountain on the coast. Its top withers at the LORD's roar (Amos 1:2) and it is no place to hide (9:3).

The LORD says through Amos, "Seek me and live" (5:4) and "Seek the LORD and live" (5:6), and not Bethel, Gilgal or Beersheba. Seek what is good, not what is evil, so that you may live (5:14). The Talmud makes the verse a summary of the commandments (Makkot 23b-24a).

sections.h: A famine of hearing the words of the LORD
sections.b: Amos 8:11-12 says the LORD will send a famine for hearing his words, and people will roam from sea to sea looking for it. Amos 3:8 says he has spoken and so the prophet must speak.

The LORD hates festivals, rejects offerings and will not listen to songs (Amos 5:21-23). The fault is worship that does not come with justice. Amos 4:4-5 mocks the zeal of the pilgrims, and 5:24 asks for justice to roll like water. Christians and Jews have read the passage as a rebuke to empty ritual, not a rejection of sacrifice.

Amos 9:2 says that if the people dig down to Sheol, the LORD's hand will take them from there. The verse sits with Psalm 139:8 and Job 11:8 as a statement that the world of the dead is not outside the LORD's reach.

Amos asks the Lord GOD to forgive and stop locusts and fire, because Jacob is small, and is heard twice (Amos 7:2-3, 5-6). In the next visions no prayer is offered (7:8; 8:2). Compare Moses (Exodus 32:11-14), Samuel and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 14:11).

The LORD rejects burnt offerings, grain offerings and peace offerings (Amos 5:22), and asks if Israel brought sacrifices in the wilderness (5:25). Amos 4:4-5 mocks the thank offering with leavened bread and the freewill offerings.
Amos has little on idols, but 5:26 names Sikkuth and Kiyyun (astral deities) and 8:14 the oaths by Dan and Beersheba. Acts 7:42-43 quotes the passage as a charge of idolatry in the wilderness.

The last verses of Amos promise that the LORD will plant Israel in its own soil and that it will never again be pulled up from the land he gave (Amos 9:14-15). Jewish, dispensational and amillennial readers disagree about how and when the promise is fulfilled.

Amos 3:7 says the Lord GOD does nothing without showing his sod (council, secret counsel) to his servants the prophets. The word is used elsewhere for the heavenly assembly (Jeremiah 23:18, 22; Job 15:8).

Amos 3:6 asks whether disaster comes to a city unless the LORD has done it. The verse is cited with Isaiah 45:7 and Lamentations 3:38 in discussions of God and evil. It speaks of calamity as judgment, not of moral evil.

sections.h: "You did not turn back to me"
sections.b: Five times Amos reports that the LORD sent a disaster and Israel "did not turn back" (4:6-11). The verb is shuv. The refrain says that each disaster was meant to bring repentance.
People are sold for a pair of sandals and coats are kept in pledge (Amos 2:6, 8; 8:6). The Torah regulates both (Exodus 22:25-27; Deuteronomy 24:10-13; Leviticus 25:39-43).

"A man and his father go in to the same young woman" is one of the charges against Israel. The Hebrew does not say whether she is a slave, a hired worker, a cult figure or a daughter-in-law. In each case she is the one without power.
The fifth disaster is an overthrow "the way God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah", and the survivors are a log snatched from the blaze (Amos 4:11).
Amos 5:1-3 is a qinah, a funeral song, sung for Israel while it is alive. Compare Lamentations and 2 Samuel 1.
The LORD raised up Nazirites as he raised prophets, and Israel made the Nazirites drink wine (Amos 2:11-12). The law is in Numbers 6.
Amos tells his hearers to go to Gilgal and rebel (4:4), not to seek it (5:5), and says it will surely go into exile (5:5). Hosea speaks of Gilgal in the same way (Hosea 4:15; 12:11).

The exodus from Egypt is the first fact in the LORD's case against Israel (2:10; 3:1) and Amos twists it: the LORD "passes through" Israel (5:17), and he also brought the Philistines and Arameans (9:7).

Amos 1:2 and Joel 3:16 are the same Hebrew line (the LORD roars from Zion and gives out his voice from Jerusalem), and the Plain gives them the same English. Amos 9:13 and Joel 3:18 share the Hebrew words for "the mountains drip sweet wine", but the verbs differ (Amos has the causative form) and so does the next clause, so the two verses are not identical. Amos 9:12 ends with "the remnant of Edom", and Obadiah is the book about Edom; Amos 1:11-12 already charges Edom with chasing his brother. Whether these links come from one writer quoting another, from a shared stock of phrases, or from an editor who tied the Twelve together is debated. In the Hebrew order Amos stands third, between Joel and Obadiah; in the Greek order it is second, after Hosea.
